title: Your client still hasn’t paid your freelance invoice. Now what?
snippet: Send a short, specific reminder today. Include the invoice number, amount and original due date, then ask your client to confirm when payment will be made. Keep the tone warm, but do not leave the action vague. The post Your client still hasn’t paid your freelance invoice. Now what? appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Treat the payment as a business commitment, however well you get on with the client. 

Include the invoice number, amount, due date and next action in every reminder. 

Increase the clarity of each follow-up rather than increasing the emotion. 

Put any revised payment date or instalment arrangement in writing. 

Agree the scope, payment stages, revisions and additional charges before the next project begins. 

Chasing a client can feel as though the reminder carries a second message: will asking again make you look difficult, or put future work at risk? That’s why it feels natural to delay the conversation, soften the request until it is difficult to understand, or hope the payment will arrive without having to chase again. 

But silence doesn’t protect the relationship. It leaves the invoice unresolved and gives frustration more time to build. You can keep the tone friendly, but the payment conversation still needs structure. Clarity can be kinder than softness because it gives both of you the best way to resolve the problem. 

This article gives general guidance for UK freelancers. Contracts, clients, and recovery options vary, so obtain appropriate legal or credit-control advice before taking formal action. 

Here are our tips:

Check the facts before choosing your tone

Spend five minutes establishing what has happened. Check that the invoice reached the right person, the payment date has passed, the amount and bank details are correct, and no query about the work remains unanswered. Note any payment date your client has already promised. 

If you didn’t agree a payment date, check the position before describing the invoice as late. For many business transactions, GOV.UK says payment must usually be made within 30 days of the customer receiving the invoice or the goods or service. Read the current payment obligations guidance and consider the actual agreement and parties involved. 

Once the facts are clear, match the message to the stage of the problem. A forgotten invoice needs a reminder. A vague promise needs a date. Repeated silence needs a final request and a decision about what you are prepared to do next. 

If your client disputes the work or amount, stop treating the problem as a simple payment delay. Ask them to explain the issue specifically and in writing, then compare it with the agreed scope and fee. Don’t reduce or abandon the invoice simply to avoid discomfort; obtain advice if the disagreement is substantial. 

Use a three-message sequence

Here’s a suggestion of how to proceed.

1. Send a friendly reminder

Use this when the agreed due date has passed and payment has not arrived. 

Hi [name], I’m following up on invoice [number] for £[amount], which was due on [date]. I haven’t received the payment yet. Could you confirm when it will be made? I’ve attached the invoice again. Thanks. 

The question asks for an outcome. ‘Could you take a look?’ may only produce another vague reply, while ‘Could you confirm when payment will be made?’ requires a date or an explanation. 

2. Ask for a specific date

If the first message produces silence or an unclear answer, make the next action and deadline explicit. 

Hi [name], I’m following up again on invoice [number] for £[amount], due on [date]. Please arrange payment or confirm a specific payment date by [date]. If there is a problem with the invoice, let me know by then so we can address it. 

The message is firmer because it removes ambiguity, not because you’re being hostile. All you are doing is asking a client to pay, identify a genuine problem or make a concrete commitment. 

3. Send a final payment request

When reminders have been ignored or commitments missed, state that this is the final request before you consider further action. 

Hi [name], this is my final payment request for invoice [number] for £[amount], which was due on [date]. Please make payment by [new date], or contact me by then with a clear proposal. If I do not hear from you, I will need to consider the appropriate next steps for recovering the outstanding payment. 

Only name a formal step that you are genuinely prepared to take. Don’t threaten court action, interest or additional charges simply to make the message sound serious. 

Use the usual channel but keep a written record

A first nudge on whatever channel you normally use with that client, even a messaging app, can be reasonable. Attach or link to the invoice so the request is easy to act on. If the first informal reminder is ignored, move the follow-up to email or another suitable written channel. 

After a call or conversation, send a short written confirmation of what was agreed. Record the outstanding balance, any instalment amounts and every payment date. This is useful for both of you and avoids relying on different memories later. 

Do not apologise for the payment itself

You can be courteous without writing ‘Sorry to bother you’ or ‘Don’t worry if you can’t do it yet’. Those phrases can make an agreed payment sound optional. Use a warm greeting or closing if that’s your usual tone with the client, but keep the request itself factual: ‘I’m following up on…’ or ‘Please confirm…’. 

If your client says they cannot pay

Ask for a proposal rather than accepting an indefinite promise. If you are willing and able to consider instalments, ask them to state the amount and date of each payment. You can then decide whether the arrangement works for you. 

Thanks for letting me know. Please send me a proposed payment plan showing the amount and date of each instalment. I’ll confirm in writing whether that arrangement works for me. 

Offering more time is a commercial decision, not something you owe any client automatically. If you agree, record the revised balance and dates in writing, and decide in advance what you will do if the plan is missed. 

Know when the conversation becomes formal

For qualifying business-to-business debts, UK rules may allow statutory interest and recovery costs. GOV.UK currently describes statutory interest as 8% plus the Bank of England base rate unless the contract sets a different rate. Check the late commercial payment rules carefully because they do not apply to every client or agreement. 

If you are a UK small business with an unresolved dispute involving a larger customer, the Small Business Commissioner may be able to help. A county court claim is another possible route in England and Wales, although GOV.UK notes that mediation may be quicker and cheaper. Scotland and Northern Ireland use different processes. 

These options change the nature of the dispute. Review the contract, evidence, value of the debt and likely costs, then obtain advice before choosing one. A long-standing or valuable client relationship doesn’t remove the debt, but it may understandably affect how you choose to resolve the situation. 

Make the next project easier

Move the money conversation to the start of the project. Agree the deliverables, total fee, deposit or payment stages, due dates, included revisions, additional-work charges and relevant production expenses. Creative work may also require clear usage or licensing terms. 

When the scope changes, describe the commercial effect before doing the extra work: ‘Happy to help. That sits outside the agreed scope, so I’ll send the additional fee and timing before I begin.’ Written terms aren’t a sign of distrust. They reduce the chance of two people remembering the same conversation differently. 

Final thoughts

For a broader process covering payment terms, deposits, follow-up and recovery measures, read the Sage guide to getting clients to pay on time. 

For the invoice in front of you now, stop rewriting the message. Confirm the amount and due date, choose the stage that matches the situation, attach the invoice and send it. 

A clear request gives you a better chance of resolving the payment before unspoken frustration becomes the larger problem. 

This article provides general information for UK freelancers and is not legal or financial advice. Payment rights, contracts and recovery procedures depend on the parties and circumstances. Check current official guidance and seek appropriate professional advice before taking formal action. 

Frequently asked questions 

			

			

	

How do I politely remind a client to pay an invoice? 

	

			

State the invoice number, amount and original due date, attach the invoice again and ask when payment will be made. A specific, courteous request is easier to act on than an indirect hint or a long explanation. 

	

	

Should I apologise when chasing payment? 

	

			

You do not need to apologise for following up on an agreed payment. Keep the greeting and closing warm if appropriate, but make the request itself factual. 

	

	

When should I send a firmer reminder? 

	

			

Send one when the first reminder has not produced payment or a specific commitment. Use the terms and circumstances to choose a reasonable deadline, but do not let repeated vague replies replace an agreed payment date. 

	

	

Can I charge interest on an overdue freelance invoice? 

	

			

You may have that right for a qualifying business-to-business debt, subject to the contract and current late-payment rules. Confirm that the rules apply before adding interest or recovery costs, and consider obtaining professional advice. 

	

	

What if my client genuinely cannot pay? 

	

			

Ask for a written proposal with specific instalment amounts and dates. You can decide whether to accept it. Record any revised arrangement and what will happen if a payment is missed.

title: I’ve been paid—how much of the money can I actually spend?
snippet: When a client payment lands, your balance can look reassuringly healthy. Before you spend it, work out what is already committed to tax, costs and the quieter weeks ahead. The post I’ve been paid—how much of the money can I actually spend? appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

A client payment is not a spending limit. First account for VAT, tax, committed costs and the likely gap before your next payment. 

There is no tax percentage that works for every freelancer. Base your reserve on current year-to-date figures and your own circumstances. 

Your bank balance can overstate what is available when supplier bills, collaborators, subscriptions or other costs have not yet been paid. 

A deliberate personal transfer—regular or variable—is safer than letting each large invoice set your spending for the month. 

If the honest remainder is repeatedly too small, treat it as evidence to revisit rates, scope, payment terms or costs. 

The notification arrives: your client has paid. Your balance looks healthier and the immediate pressure eases. Then comes the harder question: how much of that payment can you actually spend? 

For a UK sole trader, the practical answer is: only what remains after allowing for VAT, setting aside a realistic tax reserve, identifying costs already committed and leaving enough cash to reach the next likely payment. That decision needs current records and a view of what is due next—not just the latest invoice or bank balance. 

This article focuses mainly on UK self-employed sole traders. A limited company is legally separate from its owner, and taking money out through salary, dividends or a director’s loan follows different rules. See GOV.UK guidance on taking money out of a limited company. 

The balance is not the spending limit 

For an employee, Income Tax and National Insurance are usually deducted before salary reaches their bank account. As a freelancer, you may receive the full value of an invoice and have to make the important decisions afterwards. 

A large payment may represent several weeks of work rather than one unusually successful day. The next commission may be smaller, delayed or unconfirmed. The apparent surplus may also need to cover illness, holidays or time spent finding new work. 

Australia-based freelancer Rosalyn Page separates money for tax, retirement, sick leave, annual leave and business costs before looking at the remainder. The rules differ in the UK, but the emotional effect will be familiar. 

“Using this system I often feel a bit disappointed when I see what’s left over,” she says. 

She calls it a reality check. A freelance rate may look high because it covers more than the hours spent producing the work, including obligations and benefits an employer might otherwise handle. The fee is doing several jobs before any personal spending begins. 

One payment can have several jobs 

A self-employed beauty studio owner featured in Money Diaries from Sage shows what this looks like in practice. In one week, £1,037.77 came into the business. It was not all hers to spend. 

In the beauty studio owner’s Money Diary, she counted £833.71 as spent or allocated. That included £395 reserved for future rent and tax and a £300 weekly payment to herself. After the week’s other business spending, £204.06 was added to the business balance. 

She had previously varied her personal income according to each week’s takings. Later, she introduced a regular transfer: “I now pay myself £300 per week regardless of how much or how little I earn that week.” 

Her amounts are not a formula for every freelancer. The reusable part is the decision: she gave the money different jobs before treating any of it as available for personal spending. A strong week no longer set her personal budget on its own. 

Money received is not personal spending money 

Three figures are easily confused: 

Money received is the cash that has arrived from a client. If you are VAT registered, it may include VAT you charged on the invoice. 

Profit is broadly what remains after allowable business expenses. For a sole trader, taxable profit—not the amount transferred personally—is central to the tax calculation. 

Available personal spending money is the cash you can take after allowing for tax, upcoming costs and the amount the business needs to retain. 

Suppose a photographer receives £3,000 for a commission. It may need to cover an assistant, travel and equipment hire, and could be the final payment for several weeks of work. It is £3,000 received—not automatically £3,000 of profit or personal income. 

For a sole trader, a personal transfer is not an allowable business expense and does not reduce taxable profit. Our practical guide to allowable expenses for self-employed people explains which business costs you may be able to deduct when calculating your taxable profit. 

Sense-checking a payment

What already has a claim on the payment 

Here’s what you need to consider.

Tax and VAT 

A single invoice cannot tell you how much tax to reserve. For a sole trader, Income Tax and National Insurance depend on taxable profit across the year, other income and personal circumstances. A percentage can be a working estimate, but it should come from current figures—not somebody else’s rule of thumb. 

The timing matters too. Payments on account can mean paying towards the next Self Assessment bill as well as settling a balancing payment. Check your HMRC account, software or accountant’s estimate before treating the reserve as spare cash. 

If you are VAT registered, the payment may include VAT you charged. Your VAT return determines what is payable after the relevant calculations, including eligible VAT you can reclaim. Until then, do not treat the VAT-inclusive balance as personal income. See GOV.UK guidance on charging and recording VAT. 

UK freelance writer and sole trader Dan Raywood uses a deliberately cautious rule of thumb. 

“When I started as a full-time freelancer, I was told to put aside a third of every earning. I’ve also heard about putting aside a quarter, but I err on the side of caution.” 

Dan’s approach provides a starting buffer rather than calculating his eventual liability. Your appropriate reserve may be higher or lower, so compare any percentage with current year-to-date figures and your expected tax bill. 

Business costs not yet paid 

Freelance costs do not always leave the account when the related income arrives. A collaborator may invoice later; software, insurance or a membership may renew next month; materials or travel may still need to be recorded. 

A London plumber in another Money Diary used merchant accounts to buy expensive materials before paying for them. His warning was that delayed supplier bills could make the business look richer than it was. The same problem arises whenever a committed cost has not yet reached the bank statement. 

An allowable expense may reduce taxable profit, but it still consumes cash. Both its tax treatment and payment date matter. 

Personal income and a buffer 

A large invoice can make a generous personal transfer feel affordable, but that transfer still needs to work when the following month is quieter. 

Dan uses separate accounts to make those boundaries visible. 

“I use a separate account to ‘hold’ the money I earn, and put an amount each time into another account for my tax return,” he says. 

The retained balance also helped during a quieter summer. Dan made sure each month held enough to cover his bills and living costs instead of allowing one stronger invoice to set his immediate spending. 

His arrangement is a personal cash-management system, not a universal formula. You might transfer a regular amount and review it against several months of results, or vary withdrawals while maintaining a minimum balance for known commitments. Separate accounts can make reserved money harder to spend accidentally, but they do not replace accurate records or an up-to-date tax estimate. 

What if there is not enough left? 

An honest calculation may leave less than you hoped. Do not improve it on paper by deleting the tax reserve, ignoring a supplier bill or assuming a client will pay early. 

Look upstream. Your rate may not cover the full cost of freelancing; the scope may have grown without the fee changing; payment terms may leave you carrying costs too long; or overheads may be squeezing personal income. Compare several months of real records before deciding which explanation fits. 

The beauty studio owner planned to review her £300 weekly payment after six months and adjust it if the business could not support it or had room for more. Choose a method, then test it against what happens rather than treating the first figure as permanent. 

Final thoughts

We always love a client payment, but the useful number is the remainder after tax, committed costs, personal income and the next gap between payments are visible. It may look disappointing, but it is also more honest. If it repeatedly falls short, you have evidence to revisit rates, scope, payment terms or costs before the tax bill or quiet month arrives. 

This article provides general information for UK freelancers and is not personal tax, accounting or financial advice. Rules and circumstances vary, so check current GOV.UK guidance or speak to a qualified adviser if you are unsure. 

Frequently asked questions 

			

			

	

Can I spend the full value of a freelance invoice? 

	

			

Usually not. First identify any VAT included, update your tax estimate, list costs already committed and decide what the business must retain until the next expected payment. The safe-to-spend amount is the remainder—not the headline value of the invoice or the current bank balance. 

	

	

How much should a freelancer put aside for tax? 

	

			

There is no percentage that fits every freelancer. For a UK sole trader, the amount depends on taxable profit across the year, other income and personal circumstances. Use current records, allow for payments on account where relevant, and check the estimate in your software, HMRC account or with an accountant. 

	

	

Does VAT count as income? 

	

			

If you are VAT registered, the VAT collected from a customer should not be treated as personal spending money. Your VAT return determines what is payable after the relevant calculations, including eligible VAT you can reclaim. Keep the gross payment and the amount actually available to the business conceptually separate. See GOV.UK VAT guidance. 

	

	

Should I pay myself a regular amount? 

	

			

A regular transfer can make personal budgeting steadier and stop a strong month from inflating your spending. A variable amount may suit an irregular business better. Whichever approach you use, base it on several months of income and costs, retain enough for known commitments and review the figure rather than assuming it will always remain affordable. 

	

	

What changes if I work through a limited company? 

	

			

A limited company is legally separate from its owner. Company money does not automatically become personal money when a client pays. Taking money out through salary, dividends, expense repayments or a director’s loan follows different rules, so use the company’s current figures and get advice when needed. See GOV.UK guidance on taking money out of a limited company.

title: How much should a freelancer put aside for tax?
snippet: There is no safe percentage that works for every freelancer. Use your current income, allowable expenses and wider circumstances to estimate the bill, then turn that estimate into a reserve you review during the year. The post How much should a freelancer put aside for tax? appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Start with an estimate of your own tax position rather than copying another freelancer’s percentage. 

Base the estimate on taxable profit across the year and your wider income, not the value of one invoice. 

Check whether payments on account could make a January payment larger than the bill you first expected. 

Keep the reserve separate and review it monthly, quarterly or whenever your income changes materially. 

If the reserve is short, confirm the amount and act early instead of waiting for the payment deadline. 

Freelance tax anxiety often comes from not knowing the number until late in the year. A strong month can make your savings look comfortable, while a quiet spell or an unexpectedly large Self Assessment payment exposes the gap. 

The practical question is not, ‘What percentage do other freelancers save?’ 

It is, ‘What might I owe, and how much have I already put towards it?’ 

This article focuses on UK self-employed sole traders. Limited companies have a different legal and tax position. Your circumstances can also affect the calculation, so treat the process below as general planning guidance rather than personal tax advice. 

The first bill can change your habits 

Róisín Killeen, a freelance writer who contributes to Sage Advice Ireland, remembers the end of her first full year of freelancing clearly. 

“The tax bill at the end of my first year working full-time as a freelance writer was a very unpleasant surprise and one I had not budgeted for properly. The lesson was hard-learned, and since then, I am disciplined about regularly sending payments to Revenue throughout the year, which are then offset against my final yearly tax bill. This ensures that I’m in a position to pay, without having heart palpitations!” 

Róisín deals with Ireland’s Revenue rather than HMRC, so UK freelancers should not copy the payment mechanism without checking the rules that apply to them. The underlying habit is still useful: deal with tax throughout the year instead of treating the deadline as the moment to start finding the money. 

There is no universal tax percentage 

Two freelancers can receive the same £2,000 client payment and need to reserve different amounts. One may earn everything from freelance work. Another may have a salary taxed through PAYE. Their allowable expenses, other income, student loan position, available allowances and previous tax payments may also differ. 

Where you live in the UK can matter too, and a sole trader should not apply limited-company tax assumptions to their own position. One invoice cannot carry all that information. 

A percentage can still be a useful transfer habit. Once you have estimated what you are likely to owe, you can convert the remaining requirement into a working percentage or regular amount. The estimate comes first; the percentage is simply a convenient way to fund it. 

Build your tax reserve in four steps 

Here are four easy steps to ensure you keep a good tax reserve amount. 

1. Update your income and expense records 

Bring your freelance records up to date and estimate what you reasonably expect for the rest of the tax year. Include the different ways your creative work earns money, such as project fees, retainers, licensing or other commercial income. Treat possible commissions cautiously until they are confirmed. 

Keep invoices issued and payments received distinct. A sent invoice is not cash you can transfer into the reserve, while the point at which income enters your tax records depends on the accounting method you use. 

Record business costs, but do not assume every work-related purchase is automatically allowable. HMRC explains which expenses self-employed people may be able to claim. Allowable expenses can reduce taxable profit; they do not normally reduce your tax bill by the full amount you spent. 

2. Estimate your likely bill 

Use the updated figures to estimate your annual taxable profit and wider tax position. Include relevant employment or other income and tax already deducted, rather than calculating freelance work in isolation. 

You can use accounting software, work with an accountant or use HMRC’s Self Assessment tax-bill estimator. Check which tax year the tool covers and read its limitations. HMRC’s estimator does not account for every income type, payment or charge, so its result may need adjusting. 

Treat the result as a planning estimate. It should become more accurate as your records and forecast improve, but it is not a guaranteed final bill. 

3. Check payments on account 

Payments on account are advance payments towards a future Self Assessment bill, including Class 4 National Insurance where applicable. When they apply, they are normally paid in two instalments, due on 31 January and 31 July, and each is usually half the relevant tax owed for the previous year. 

They do not apply to everyone. Under current payments-on-account rules, they are generally not required if the previous Self Assessment bill was below £1,000 or more than 80% of the tax was collected outside Self Assessment. Your statement or online account should show whether you need to make them. 

The first January in which payments on account apply can be surprising because the amount due may include the bill for the year just reported and the first advance payment towards the next one. Check whether your estimate already includes that advance before adding it, or you could count the same amount twice. 

If you expect your income—and therefore your tax bill—to be lower than the previous year, you can ask HMRC to reduce your payments on account. However, if you reduce them too far and the eventual bill is higher than expected, HMRC will charge interest on the difference. 

4. Compare the estimate with your reserve 

Compare the provisional amount you expect to need with relevant tax already paid and the money already in your tax pot. The difference is your current reserve gap. 

Start with the estimated Income Tax and National Insurance requirement. 

Add expected payments on account only if they are not already included. 

Subtract relevant tax payments or credits already reflected in your position. 

Subtract the money already reserved. 

Write down what each figure includes. A single source of truth reduces the risk of adding or subtracting the same payment twice. 

A simple reserve example 

Imagine Maya is a self-employed illustrator. Her provisional Income Tax and National Insurance estimate is £4,000. She also expects a first payment on account of £2,000 that is not included in that estimate. Her tax pot currently holds £3,500. 

Her provisional requirement is £6,000. After subtracting the £3,500 already reserved, her current gap is £2,500. She can use that figure to plan transfers from confirmed client payments, then repeat the comparison when her income or expenses change. 

The figures illustrate reserve planning, not the tax due at a particular income level. Maya’s £4,000 estimate would need to come from an appropriate calculation using her actual circumstances. 

Keep the reserve separate and keep it current 

A separate account or clearly labelled bank pot makes the boundary between reserved money and spending money easier to see. Moving money when a client payment clears can also prevent the full balance from feeling available. 

The separate account does not decide how much you owe. Review the reserve monthly or quarterly, and whenever something material changes: a large contract arrives, work drops away, you start or leave employment, or your costs shift significantly. 

If the latest estimate suggests you have reserved too much, check that all relevant income, charges and forthcoming payments are included before treating the apparent surplus as spendable. 

If the reserve is already short 

Update the records and confirm the gap first. That replaces a vague sense of impending doom with a number you can plan around. You may be able to reduce it across the remaining months or the client payments you realistically expect to receive. 

If you cannot pay the bill in full, do not wait for the deadline to pass. HMRC says some people may be able to set up a payment plan based on what they can afford. Contact HMRC or an appropriately qualified adviser promptly and check the current conditions rather than assuming somebody else’s arrangement will apply to you. 

Final thoughts

The most useful answer to ‘How much should I put aside?’ is not a percentage. It is the current gap between a defensible estimate and the money already reserved. Keep that gap visible and update it before it becomes a deadline problem. 

This article provides general information for UK freelancers and is not personal tax, accounting or financial advice. Tax rules and individual circumstances vary and can change. Check current HMRC guidance or consult an appropriately qualified professional before acting. 

Frequently asked questions 

			

			

	

Is 20 percent or 30 percent enough to save for freelance tax? 

	

			

It may be enough for one freelancer and wrong for another. Test any percentage against an estimate based on your annual taxable profit, other income, circumstances and expected payments on account. Review it when those inputs change. 

	

	

Should I put tax aside from every invoice? 

	

			

Moving money whenever a client payment clears can be a useful habit, especially with irregular income. The amount should still come from your latest estimate rather than an arbitrary rule of thumb. 

	

	

Do allowable expenses reduce the amount of tax I owe? 

	

			

Allowable expenses can reduce the taxable profit used in the calculation. They do not usually reduce the final tax bill by the full cost of the purchase, and recording a cost does not automatically make it allowable. 

	

	

Why can a January Self Assessment payment be larger than expected? 

	

			

The amount may include a balancing payment for the year already reported and the first payment on account towards the following year. Check your Self Assessment statement and whether your estimate already includes both elements. 

	

	

How often should I update my tax reserve? 

	

			

A monthly or quarterly review is a practical baseline. Update it sooner after a significant change in income, expenses, employment or another part of your tax position.

title: Can I afford this? A freelancer’s guide to spending during a quiet month
snippet: When work slows down, even a small purchase can feel difficult to judge. Here’s how to check what you can afford, protect essential costs and decide what can wait. The post Can I afford this? A freelancer’s guide to spending during a quiet month appeared first on Sage Advice UK.
fullText:
Key takeaways

Check what your money already needs to cover before treating it as available. 

Test a purchase against delayed payments, not just your expected income. 

Decide whether a purchase is essential, a business investment or optional. 

Include renewals, repayments and other future commitments in the cost. 

Set a review date for postponed purchases so you don’t reconsider them every day. 

You’ve had fewer enquiries this month. A project has moved back and a regular client hasn’t confirmed their next brief. 

Then your laptop starts struggling, a course goes on sale or a friend suggests a weekend away. You have money in the bank, but how much of it can you really afford to spend? 

Start with the commitments behind your balance. Once you know what’s covered and what remains uncertain, you can judge the purchase itself. 

Here’s what we discuss in this article:

Work out what is available 

Choose a period to look ahead: perhaps until the next expected payment, with extra time allowed for a delay. 

List the essential household costs and business commitments falling due in that period. Include annual bills and any project costs you’ve already agreed to pay. 

MoneyHelper’s guidance on irregular income recommends identifying regular outgoings and planning for higher-cost periods as well as seasonal changes in earnings.  

Keep tax money separate from the amount you treat as available. If you’ve already assigned money to future costs, don’t count it twice. 

Here’s an illustrative check for a sole trader, combining the money available for their business and household: 

Item

Amount

Total cash across accounts included in this check 

£4,200 

Less tax reserve included in that total 

£900 

Less essential household costs for the period 

£1,700 

Less committed business costs for the period 

£500 

Less buffer to retain beyond the period 

£800 

Amount remaining after planned commitments and buffer 

£300 

The £300 is a planning figure, rather than a guarantee. It depends on whether the costs are complete and the period is long enough. 

If tax reserves sit in a separate account excluded from your starting figure, don’t subtract them again. Likewise, exclude transfers between your own accounts from spending totals. 

You may decide you can afford a £40 purchase from that remainder. A £600 purchase needs a different plan, such as a cheaper option, a repair or waiting for a payment to arrive. 

Check what changes if a payment is late 

An invoice due next week can make a purchase look affordable. But would it still work if your client paid a fortnight later? 

First, check why money is tight. Have you had less paid work, or are you waiting for clients to pay for work you’ve already delivered? Both can restrict spending. You may need to review your income outlook, follow up outstanding invoices, or do both. 

Run two versions of your spending check: one with the expected payment and one with it delayed. 

For example, if a £500 purchase only works when an invoice arrives exactly on time, the decision depends on that payment. Check which essential costs would be left uncovered if it slipped. 

As we explored in the hidden hours behind late payments, getting paid can itself create extra work. Check whether the client has received your invoice, whether anything is holding up approval and when payment is expected. Until the money arrives, keep the delayed-payment scenario in your plan. 

Keep unconfirmed projects outside the money you rely on. An encouraging conversation isn’t yet an agreed commission. 

If a discretionary purchase would put essentials at risk when a payment slips, waiting is a practical choice. Decide what would need to happen before you reconsider it: payment received or another cost reduced. 

If the purchase is urgent, investigate the least costly way to meet the need. Could you repair a laptop, rent equipment for a particular job or use a tool you already have? 

The aim is to preserve your ability to work while protecting the commitments you can’t postpone. 

Decide what the purchase does for you 

Not all spending has the same purpose. Ask which of these best describes the purchase. 

It keeps essential work or life running 

Food, housing and equipment delivering an agreed project need a different decision from an optional upgrade. 

If essential costs aren’t covered, pause discretionary spending and identify the shortfall. Contact affected providers early and seek support if you’re struggling with bills. 

It could improve the business 

A course, software tool or portfolio update may be worthwhile. Make the benefit specific. 

Will it help deliver confirmed work? Replace another cost? Address a skill clients already ask for? Or is the hoped-for return much less certain? 

In the Money Diary of a beauty studio owner, the owner describes paying for a booking system that reduces the need for clients to contact her to arrange or change appointments.  

That offers a useful question for a creative freelancer considering software: which task will this remove, and how much will that matter to your work? 

During a quiet period, having spare time to learn something also doesn’t necessarily mean having spare money to buy it. 

Sometimes, the cost of doing something yourself matters too. 

At the SMB Advisory Board in September 2026, formed by Sage, self-employed handyman Josh explained that he had turned down jobs to complete his first Making Tax Digital submission. The experience convinced him that paying for accountant support was worthwhile. 

He was talking about tax administration rather than quiet-month spending, but the principle is useful when weighing an investment: what will doing without it cost you in time, work or disruption? That benefit still needs to fit what you can afford today. 

It’s something you want for yourself 

You don’t have to justify every personal purchase as business development. 

A modest leisure budget can be part of your plan if essentials and the reserve you need remain covered. Set an amount you can afford, rather than repeatedly deciding whether each coffee or outing is acceptable. 

If there is no room this month, acknowledge that limit and choose when you’ll review it. The decision can change when the numbers do. 

Look beyond the price today 

A £25 monthly subscription costs £300 over a year. A discounted course may need extra software, and new equipment can bring insurance, accessories or maintenance. Check the full cost, the cancellation terms and what the purchase commits you to next. 

Keep affordability separate from tax treatment

Spreading the cost doesn’t make it cheaper. If you’re considering a credit card, buy now, pay later or equipment finance, include every future repayment in your check, and test it against a late payment too. 

Also keep affordability separate from tax treatment. Something may qualify as an allowable expense and still leave you short of money. Our guide to allowable expenses explains the claiming rules.  

Make a decision and set a review date 

Once you’ve checked the numbers, choose a clear next step: 

Buy now: The need is clear and the cost fits your plan. 

Choose a smaller option: Meet the need with less cash or a shorter commitment. 

Wait for a trigger: Reconsider when a payment arrives or work is confirmed. 

Leave it: The benefit doesn’t justify the cost. 

For anything postponed, record the reason and a date or condition for reviewing it. 

That could be: “Review the course after the overdue invoice is paid” or “Recheck the laptop budget at the end of the month; arrange a repair meanwhile.” 

Repeat the check when income, bills or deadlines change. You don’t need to reopen it every time you see the same offer. 

Final thoughts

Choose one purchase you’re considering now. Check it against the money left after commitments, then test what happens if your next payment is late. 

You’ll have a clearer reason to buy, wait or choose something cheaper. 

FAQs about quiet-month spending 

			

			

	

How do I know if I can afford something when freelance income is unpredictable? 

	

			

Subtract tax, essential costs and your buffer from your balance, then check whether the purchase still fits if your next payment is late. 

Give essential costs, reserves and discretionary spending clear places in your plan. Then judge purchases against that plan. If something needs to wait, set a review point so it remains a decision, rather than an ongoing worry. 

		

	

	

Should I stop all non-essential spending when work slows down? 

	

			

Not necessarily. Check the numbers first. If essentials and your planned reserve are covered, some discretionary spending may fit. If there is a shortfall, prioritise addressing it before adding optional costs. 

	

	

Can I spend money from my quiet-month buffer? 

	

			

Yes, that’s what it’s for. Use it for the costs it was meant to cover, check what’s left, and keep tax money separate. 

	

	

Should I buy a course while I have more time? 

	

			

Only if it meets a specific business need and you can afford the full cost. Spare time makes learning possible, but doesn’t establish that a paid course is the best option. 

	

	

What if I need equipment to complete a paid project? 

	

			

Compare repair, rental, borrowing and replacement options. Check when the client will pay and whether agreed staged payments could help cover project costs. Confirm any changed terms before relying on them.
